summary: This document covers the CAPWAP binding for IEEE 802.11, which defines two MAC modes for wireless transmission points: Split MAC and Local MAC. It describes how the 802.11 MAC functions are divided between the access point and the controller in each mode.

plainLanguage.summary: A wireless access point and its central controller must share the work. This describes two ways of dividing the jobs between them.

questions: capwap split mac vs local mac
where does 802.11 encryption happen in capwap
subtitle: A way for a wireless controller to tell an access point exactly where Wi-Fi encryption happens.

tldr.problem: In CAPWAP Split MAC mode, IEEE 802.11 encryption could sit in either the access controller or the access point, with no clear way to say which, so equipment from different vendors did not interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: Two new message elements let the access point list the MAC profiles it supports and let the controller pick one, each profile placing encryption and decryption unambiguously at the WTP (profile 0) or the AC (profile 1).
tldr.outcome: Operators get a defined negotiation instead of vendor-specific configuration, and the security considerations match those of RFC 5416.

today: RFC 7494 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the Split MAC mode defined in RFC 5416.

sections.title: The Ambiguity in Split MAC
sections.content:
CAPWAP supports two MAC modes, Local MAC and Split MAC (RFC 5415, RFC 5416). Some MAC functions were never clearly assigned. In particular, IEEE 802.11 encryption is described as located in either the AC or the WTP, with no clear way to negotiate where.

Because vendors defined the modes differently, operators had to configure deployments differently depending on the vendor, and mixing WTPs and ACs from different vendors caused interoperability issues. Local MAC has no such problem, since encryption is always at the WTP.

The fix is the IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile, which specifies unambiguously where each MAC function is located.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody agreed who should lock the safe, so every shop did it differently and visiting staff got confused.

sections.title: The Two MAC Profiles
sections.content:
A profile describes how MAC functionality is divided between the WTP and the AC. Two are defined, and both resemble the Split MAC of RFC 5416 except for where encryption lives.

  • Profile 0, Split MAC with WTP encryption: 802.11 encryption and decryption are at the WTP. Because fragmentation is always done at the same entity as encryption, fragmentation and defragmentation are at the WTP too.
  • Profile 1, Split MAC with AC encryption: encryption and decryption are at the AC, so the AC also does fragmentation and defragmentation.

In both, the WTP handles beacon generation, probe response generation, power management and packet buffering, and queuing. The AC handles the distribution and integration services, association handling, classifying, IEEE 802.1X/EAP and RSNA key management. Scheduling differs: in profile 0 it is WTP/AC, meaning admission control is on the AC and real-time scheduling and queuing are on the WTP, while in profile 1 it is at the WTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Profile 0 says the clerk (the access point) locks the safe. Profile 1 says the manager (the controller) does. Either way, it is written down.

sections.title: The Two Message Elements
sections.content:
Two CAPWAP message elements carry the negotiation.

The IEEE 802.11 Supported MAC Profiles element (type 1060) lets the WTP list the profiles it supports. It holds a Num_Profiles field, which must be at least 1, followed by one profile value each. The Discovery Request, Primary Discovery Request and Join Request messages may include one.

The IEEE 802.11 MAC Profile element (type 1061) lets the AC select one profile. It may be provided along with the IEEE 802.11 ADD WLAN message element while configuring a WLAN on the WTP. Its single 8-bit Profile field is 0 for Split MAC with WTP encryption and 1 for Split MAC with AC encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: One form lists what the clerk is able to do. The other is the manager's answer saying which way it will be done.

sections.title: Negotiating a Profile
sections.content:
The WTP first tells the AC which profiles it supports, in either a Discovery Request or the Join Request. The AC determines the appropriate profile and configures the WTP with it while configuring the WLAN.

In the RFC's example, the WTP sends a Join Request carrying the Supported MAC Profiles, the AC answers with a Join Response, and the AC then sends an IEEE 802.11 WLAN Config. Request containing the Add WLAN and MAC Profile elements. The WTP replies with a WLAN Config. Response.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk says what they can do, and the manager replies with the chosen way when giving the clerk their first job.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the two message elements, 1060 and 1061, in the CAPWAP Message Element Type registry from RFC 5415. It also created a new subregistry, "IEEE 802.11 Split MAC Profile", for the 8-bit Profile field (0 to 255). This RFC defines values 0 and 1; the remaining values (2 to 255) are maintained by IANA under Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers now has entries for the two ways of doing it, and room to add more later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not introduce any new security risks compared to RFC 5416, whose security considerations apply here too. The negotiation messages between the WTP and the AC have origin authentication and data integrity, so an attacker cannot interfere with them to force a less-secure mode choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The note between clerk and manager is sealed and signed, so a stranger cannot change it to a weaker way of locking up.
